Article Title: Rare textile fragments have survived for around 1,300 years inside a Viking woman’s Danish grave because metallic salts released by two brooches inhibited microbes that would normally destroy the clot
Article Text:
Credit: Arkæologi Vestjylland

When metal became a time capsule

Credit: Arkæologi Vestjylland

Danish archaeologists have unearthed rare textile remains from a Viking woman's grave near Varde, in the heart of Western Jutland. During excavations at the Skonager site (ARV 661), a team of archaeologists discovered a Viking Age burial in which fragments of clothing survived against all odds. This discovery gives a rare glimpse into Viking dress from around 1,300 years ago. The fragments of wool and linen were still preserved, thanks to the two brooches that once fastened the clothing of the Viking woman. Radiocarbon dating will now determine whether she wore a newly woven dress with a repaired family heirloom, or if both pieces belonged to the same era.The discovery at Skonager in Western Jutland, Denmark, has given researchers something almost impossible to find: textile scraps from an 8th-century burial, preserved not in some ideal climate-controlled cave but in soil so acidic it normally dissolves cloth to nothing. So what prevented this? It turns out that metal became the time capsule. The two scoop brooches, with their concave shape, did the heavy lifting. The bronze and silver corroded on the woman’s skeleton, which released metallic salts into the surrounding soil. Those salts created a hostile environment, which prevented bacteria and fungi from consuming the fibres. In life, those very ornaments held her dress together, and after death, they ended up preserving it for history!The brooches were positioned to fasten the fabric across her torso.The brooches held bits of cloth clinging to both their upper and lower surfaces. The researchers can now map the construction of her garment, the outer fabric she showed the world and the inner layer against her skin, giving a sneak peek of Viking fashion from 1,300 years ago. Woven textile fragments don't come up often in Viking archaeology anywhere. The new discovery could reveal more information about the kind of fibres used, the sewing techniques and potentially the structure of female garments from 8th-century Denmark. Finding them, especially in soil, makes them one of the most miraculous discoveries of the time.The extraction and analysis of these fragile textile remains is complex. The museum in charge of this excavation has put together a top-tier multidisciplinary team to ensure that every grain of sand surrounding the remains is extracted with the meticulousness of a surgical procedure.The Vejle Conservation Center (Konserveringscenter Vejle) didn't just dig. They removed the remains particle by particle with utmost precision. One wrong move and fibres crumble. One careless shovel stroke and context vanishes. Lise Ræder Knudsen, an ancient textile specialist, will examine the recovered fibres to determine weaving patterns, thread quality and the technical skill involved in making the ancient Viking Jutland garment. All these could help to determine if the woman who wore it had access to fine cloth or made do with rougher weaves.The teeth of the young woman found were preserved in surprisingly good condition. The Anthropology Unit at the University of Southern Denmark will analyse them for clues to understand her age, health and diet. Isotope analysis of tooth enamel can reveal where she spent her childhood, whether she moved between regions and what kinds of physical stress her body endured during development.However, dating the textile remains is going to be a rather difficult task. The researchers are hoping that radiocarbon (C14) testing may help to obtain an absolute and precise dating of the textile assemblage.One of the brooches shows repair marks, suggesting it had been broken and mended sometime before ending up in this grave. That raises an archaeological puzzle: Was the brooch made at the same time as the dress, or was it inherited? If a young woman wore a newly woven garment fastened with her grandmother's jewellery, it changes how we read her burial. Radiocarbon dating of the fabric and the metal will answer whether these pieces belong to the same era or if she chose to wear old ornaments with new clothes. All these could tell us what objects meant to her community.The researchers are also hoping to find out other aspects of the cloth beyond its weave and morphology. For example, the colour. Nobody knows what colour the dress was. Dye molecules degrade faster than weave structure. Researchers have launched what they're calling the Textile Colours of the Viking Age project to find out. Ulla Mannering and Charlotte Rimstad will conduct spectral analyses of the fibres to identify any remaining organic dye compounds. If there is enough colour on the fabric, they could perhaps reconstruct the palette. Colour in Viking garments carried meaning. A wealthy woman might wear dyed textiles that signalled status. A poorer woman wore undyed wool. The hues themselves tell part of her story. It could reveal the social, economic and ritual connotations of the deceased woman.The research has funding from the Agnes Geijers Foundation, named for one of the first scholars to seriously study Viking women's clothing. Geijer made detailed drawings of what dresses held by scoop brooches might have looked like. Now, after decades of speculation based on fragmentary evidence, researchers can check whether her historical reconstructions were anywhere close to reality.
Article Summary: Danish archaeologists have unearthed rare textile remains from a Viking woman's grave near Varde, in the heart of Western Jutland. The fragments of wool and linen were still preserved, thanks to the two brooches that once fastened the clothing of the Viking woman. Radiocarbon dating will now determine whether she wore a newly woven dress with a repaired family heirloom, or if both pieces belonged to the same era.

Article Title: In 1954, aviation pioneer Glenn L. Martin donated over 2,500 acres of his Chesapeake Bay hunting preserve; today the refuge spans 4,548 acres and protects migratory birds
Article Text:
Chesapeake Bay (Image Credit: iStock)

From private preserve to refuge

A seasonal haven for birds

Beyond waterfowl

A refuge shaped by the bay

A piece of Chesapeake Bay marshland that once formed part of an aviation pioneer's private hunting preserve has become an important refuge for wildlife. What began as a donation of thousands of acres more than seven decades ago now protects tidal marshes, creeks, coves and wooded ridges used by migratory birds throughout the year. The landscape is part of a larger story of how privately held land can become a lasting habitat when it is placed under conservation management. Today, the refuge provides seasonal shelter for waterfowl, nesting grounds for numerous birds and habitat for mammals, reptiles and marine species, while also preserving a distinctive part of the Chesapeake Bay's natural landscape. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service records that Martin National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1954 after Glenn L. Martin donated 2,569 acres to the Service.The refuge occupies the northern half of Smith Island, about 11 miles west of Crisfield, Maryland, along with Watts Island farther south in the Chesapeake Bay. Its landscape is dominated by tidal marsh, with a network of creeks and coves, freshwater potholes and slightly elevated ridges supporting shrubs and trees. Offshore shallow waters also contain submerged aquatic vegetation, which provides an important food source for waterfowl.When Martin donated the property in 1954, the goal was no longer simply to preserve land for private recreation. The newly established refuge was intended to provide habitat for wildlife, particularly birds that depend on the Chesapeake Bay during migration and winter.The refuge's size has increased considerably since its creation. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Martin National Wildlife Refuge now spans 4,548 acres, following additional land purchases and donations over the years.The refuge's marshes and protected waters make it particularly valuable to migratory birds. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes the area as an important resting and wintering site for thousands of waterfowl. Winter visitors include black ducks, pintails, mergansers, long-tailed ducks, scoters, buffleheads, Canada geese and tundra swans. Historical records show that wintering waterfowl populations at the refuge could be substantial. The refuge has historically supported large numbers of wintering waterfowl, including ducks, Canada geese and tundra swans. These populations illustrate why protecting the marsh and surrounding shallow waters became an important part of refuge management.The habitat is not only important in winter. During spring and summer, marsh grasses, insects and underwater vegetation attract ducks including black ducks, mallards, gadwalls and green-winged teal for nesting. Gulls, terns, black skimmers, American oystercatchers and willets also use the marshes, mudflats and sandbars.Although migratory waterfowl are central to the refuge's purpose, the protected landscape supports a much broader community of wildlife. Wooded ridges provide nesting locations for wading birds, while groups of herons, egrets and glossy ibis have established nesting colonies. Several species, including glossy ibis, little blue herons, tricoloured herons and several egret species, have been observed in rookeries on the refuge. Martin National Wildlife Refuge also supports the largest colony of brown pelicans in Maryland's portion of Chesapeake Bay.The marshes are home to mammals including red foxes, muskrats, mink, otters and voles. Northern diamondback terrapins and various nonvenomous water snakes also inhabit the area. Clapper rails, seaside sparrows and marsh wrens depend on the marsh habitat, while peregrine falcons have nested at the refuge since the installation of a nesting tower in 1984.The conservation value of Martin National Wildlife Refuge extends beyond birds and land animals. Its marshes and estuarine waters contribute to the Chesapeake Bay food web, supporting marine organisms such as crabs and oysters. The refuge is therefore part of a much larger ecological system in which wetlands, shallow waters, vegetation and wildlife are closely connected. The land also carries a long human history. Smith Island was explored and charted by Captain John Smith in 1608, while settlers later raised cattle on parts of the island. For more than three centuries, island communities have depended on Chesapeake Bay resources, particularly oysters and crabs. Evidence of old livestock corrals and low dikes built to hold back tides remains visible in parts of the landscape.What began with Martin's 2,569-acre donation has therefore become more than a preserved piece of land. Expanded to 4,548 acres, Martin National Wildlife Refuge now protects a changing mosaic of marshes, waterways and ridges that wildlife uses throughout the year. Its history demonstrates how a single land donation can eventually become part of a much larger conservation legacy, one that continues to provide habitat for thousands of migratory birds and other species along the Chesapeake Bay.
Article Summary: Martin National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1954 after Glenn L. Martin donated 2,569 acres to the Service. The refuge provides seasonal shelter for waterfowl, nesting grounds for numerous birds and habitat for mammals, reptiles and marine species. The landscape is part of a larger story of how privately held land can become a lasting habitat.

Article Title: No surrender, no dissent: How six months of war hardened Iran’s leadership
Article Text:
Tehran’s leaders appear determined to maintain confrontation with Washington while ensuring that economic hardship does not translate into political unrest.

Tehran warns of a wider confrontation

Hardliners tighten grip around new supreme leader

Taeb appointment sends warning on dissent

Economic crisis exposes divisions inside Iran

Iran’s leadership faces a choice

Six months into its war with the United States and Israel, Iran’s leadership has tightened its grip around a core of hard-line military commanders and clerics, signalling that it will resist US pressure abroad while moving aggressively to prevent dissent at home.A series of senior appointments announced on August 11 and 12 has placed veteran Revolutionary Guard figures and security officials at the heart of Iran’s leadership. The moves come as Tehran prepares for a potentially prolonged confrontation with Washington, rejects trust in negotiations with President Donald Trump and faces mounting economic pressure from the US blockade and new sanctions.The appointments have also made clear that Iran’s rulers are preparing for unrest even as no fresh nationwide protests have emerged. The choice of Hossein Taeb, a veteran intelligence chief who has overseen major crackdowns on protests, to lead the Basij volunteer force is being viewed as a particularly strong warning to potential dissenters.Iran’s new secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, has adopted a defiant tone towards Washington.“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” Rezaei said last weekend.In a post on X, he warned that “if the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported” from the Persian Gulf.His remarks came as Iran faces the prospect of further US military action. Tehran has little faith in reaching a lasting agreement with Trump after coming under attack twice while negotiations were under way. Iranian officials are also believed to be preparing for another possible assault once Washington replenishes its stocks of missile interceptors.The threat of escalation comes alongside an increasingly severe economic squeeze. The US blockade and planned sanctions risk further damaging an economy already struggling with the impact of the war.Rezaei has nevertheless left the door open to negotiations, but only if Washington changes course. On Monday, he told Pakistani mediator Gen. Asim Munir that the US should “change its attitude and take practical action about implementing the conditions” of the ceasefire deal.Rezaei’s appointment was part of a wider reshuffle ordered by Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has been consolidating his leadership after the death of his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.The elder Khamenei, who had led Iran for about 37 years, was killed in US and Israeli strikes launched on February 28. Much of Iran’s senior leadership was also killed in the bombing campaign.The younger Khamenei, 56, has not appeared publicly or been heard in video or audio since the strikes. He is believed to have been wounded. His continued absence could reflect the extraordinary security measures around him, given that he is likely to remain an Israeli target, or the severity of his injuries.His first major appointments suggest that he is relying heavily on a group of longstanding military and security allies.Rezaei, 71, commanded the Revolutionary Guard during much of its formative period, including the 1980-1988 war with Iraq, and remained in the post until 1997. He has also contested Iran’s presidential election several times as a hard-line candidate.Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, 68, has been confirmed as head of the Revolutionary Guard after serving as acting commander since his predecessor was killed alongside the elder Khamenei. Gen. Ali Ozmaei and Gen. Ali Abdollahi have also been confirmed in senior military positions.Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Middle East office in Bahrain, described the appointments as evidence of an effort to maintain unity at the top.“They are a clique of older senior officers who’ve served together over the last decades,” Bruchmann said.“ It looks like internal cohesion, as in hard core people are being pulled into the inner circle,” he said.Perhaps the clearest indication of Tehran’s domestic priorities is the appointment of Taeb as head of the Basij, the Revolutionary Guard’s volunteer street force.The 63-year-old cleric has a long record of suppressing protests. He led the Basij during the mass demonstrations that followed the disputed 2009 re-election of hard-line president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, when dozens of people were killed.Taeb was later appointed head of the Revolutionary Guard’s intelligence organisation, a position he held for nearly 13 years before being removed in 2022. His departure reportedly followed a shake-up prompted by Israeli espionage successes.The Basij operates a nationwide network of volunteers with a presence in streets, government offices and cultural centres. Its role is to reinforce loyalty to Iran’s theocratic system and promote what the leadership describes as ideological purity.Taeb’s return to a frontline security position suggests that Tehran is preparing to confront discontent before it develops into another mass movement.“Putting someone from an intelligence background in charge of the people that would do the crackdown makes sense,” Bruchmann said.The Basij expanded its presence during the war, while hard-liners have staged nightly rallies in Tehran and other cities. The gatherings have sought to demonstrate support for the government and intimidate potential opponents.In his appointment decree, Khamenei ordered Taeb to expand the Basij’s presence in Iranian social life, make greater use of new technologies and “promote the Basij across the world against Zionist-American arrogance”. The wording could also point to a greater role for the force in building links with Iran’s overseas allies and proxies.Taeb has also warned that US economic pressure is designed to divide Iranian society.“If the mosque becomes the center of the neighborhood, the nation will protect its unity, which will be a greater deterrent than any missile.”The leadership’s increasingly hard-line posture comes as ordinary Iranians struggle with the economic consequences of the war.There has so far been no clear sign of a new nationwide protest movement, despite growing difficulties in affording basic goods. But the worsening economic situation has exposed differences within the political establishment over how far Iran should continue confronting Washington.President Masoud Pezeshkian remains one of the most prominent voices advocating a negotiated settlement. His allies have argued that Tehran risks weakening itself by prolonging the conflict while its economy deteriorates.“It would be better to bring the war to an end, since today we enjoy power and dignity and the entire world approved our victory, and the U.S. is hated,” Pezeshkian said last week.He has also defended the June ceasefire agreement, rejecting accusations from hard-liners that it gave away too much.The ceasefire quickly collapsed as the US, Israel and Iran resumed exchanges of strikes. Tehran has since demanded the release of billions of dollars in frozen assets under the agreement, along with formal authority over the Strait of Hormuz.Homayoun Falakshahi, the top oil analyst for global commerce information firm Kpler, said the latest appointments pointed to a tougher approach.The selection of Rezaei and Vahidi showed “greater influence for officials associated with a tougher stance,” he wrote.But he cautioned that escalation carries major risks for Tehran. Iran could struggle to “escalate enough to restore deterrence without triggering retaliation that leaves it worse off”.The emerging power structure therefore presents a stark contrast to Trump’s early hopes that the war could help topple Iran’s Islamic Republic and bring more conciliatory figures to power.Instead, six months of conflict have strengthened the influence of officials with decades of experience in Iran’s military and security establishment.Tehran’s leaders appear determined to maintain confrontation with Washington while ensuring that economic hardship does not translate into political unrest.The result is a leadership that is simultaneously preparing for another possible US attack, threatening retaliation and reinforcing the machinery used to suppress domestic opposition.Tehran-based political analyst Ahmad Zeidabadi said there are “serious differences over the future path of the country”.Hard-liners oppose normalisation with the US because “their survival depends on the existence of conflict and hostility,” he wrote in the newspaper Hammihan, which supports Pezeshkian.For now, the balance of power appears to favour those advocating resistance rather than compromise. Iran’s new leadership is signalling that it will not easily yield to US demands abroad, while showing that dissent at home will face an equally uncompromising response.
Article Summary: Hardliners tighten grip around new supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei. Hossein Taeb, a veteran intelligence chief who has overseen major crackdowns on protests, to lead the Basij volunteer force. New secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei has adopted a defiant tone towards Washington.

Article Title: McDonald’s-backed grants worth $2.4 million are unlocking nearly $99.1 million for conservation deals covering more than 100,650 acres of working ranches across 11 US states
Article Text: McDonald's has approximately 13,500 restaurants in US, and while the brand serves a variety of menu options across the country, it also supports other causes. On August 27, 2026, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) announced nearly $2.4 million in grants, supported by funding from McDonald's USA and several of its suppliers. The initiative aims to help complete voluntary conservation easements on working ranches across the Great Plains, Rocky Mountain West and West Coast of US, as per the NFWF website.The grants will unlock nearly $99.1 million in total conservation impact by leveraging approximately $96.7 million in matching contributions that support the advancement of conservation easements. Awarded through the Grassland Resilience and Conservation Initiative, the six grants help complete conservation easements on 31 properties across 11 states. Together, these projects will help permanently conserve more than 100,650 acres of grasslands while keeping ranching operations productive and economically viable.The landmark, seven-year initiative aims to invest more than $200 million to benefit America’s iconic grasslands, cattle ranching communities and wildlife populations that depend on healthy soils, productive habitats and plentiful water. Through this initiative, grants will promote and accelerate wildlife conservation efforts across 4 million acres of grazing lands within the Great Plains, Rocky Mountain West, Midwest, West Coast and Southeast.“This investment from the Grassland Resilience and Conservation Initiative reflects the power of collaborative conservation to protect America’s grasslands and working lands,” said Jeff Trandahl, executive director and CEO of NFWF. “These projects are designed to safeguard critical wildlife migration corridors and working lands that are essential to ranching livelihoods and thriving ecosystems. This latest round of funding demonstrates the Initiative’s continued commitment to conserving grasslands and supporting the communities that depend upon their sustained health, resilience and productivity. ”The grants announced today will help move voluntary conservation easement projects through the final stages of completion by covering transaction and due diligence costs that are essential but often difficult to fund. Conservation easements are voluntary legal agreements between landowners and land trusts or government agencies that permanently limit certain uses of a property while safeguarding its natural, scenic or agricultural value. These agreements allow landowners to retain their private property rights while simultaneously protecting intact grasslands that are the centrepiece of rural economies and the beef supply chain in the United States.Transaction and due diligence costs can include property appraisals, baseline inventory reports, environmental risk assessments and title insurance costs, essential steps that ensure voluntary conservation easements are legally and financially sound. While necessary, these costs often fall on landowners and conservation organisations and can become a costly barrier to closing a voluntary conservation easement. By covering these expenses, the grants aim to help move nearly completed projects across the finish line and fill a gap that is often overlooked by grant funding.Launched in 2025, the Grassland Resilience and Conservation Initiative is a partnership between NFWF and McDonald’s USA, some of its key beef and beverage suppliers and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS). It aims to advance voluntary conservation practices on grass-dominated landscapes in active beef cattle production across US.Voluntary conservation easements are an effective tool for keeping grasslands intact to support both wildlife habitat and livestock grazing. Many of the properties that will benefit from the grants face a high risk of conversion and represent areas of high biodiversity. Safeguarding these lands will help conserve critical habitat and migration routes for wildlife, ranging from big-game species like pronghorn and mule deer, to greater sage-grouse, burrowing owls, and other grassland birds such as the lark bunting and Baird’s sparrow. These efforts will ensure that ranching families can continue to steward intact grasslands for generations to come and preserve their way of life.
Article Summary: The National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) announced nearly $2.4 million in grants, supported by funding from McDonald's USA. The initiative aims to help complete voluntary conservation easements on working ranches across the Great Plains, Rocky Mountain West and West Coast of US.

Article Title: Researchers piecing together ancient tablets, inscriptions and a statue argue that three forgotten kings ruled Assyria more than 2,700 years ago, potentially changing part of the empire’s accepted chr
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A gap in the king list

The rebel king Tiglath-pileser

A missing Shalmaneser and a rewritten inscription

Aššur-uballiṭ and the damaged statue

What this means for Assyrian history

For more than 2,700 years, the story of Assyria’s kings has survived through fragments of clay tablets, royal inscriptions, monuments and carefully preserved lists of rulers. Together, these records have allowed historians to reconstruct the succession of one of the ancient Near East’s most powerful kingdoms. Yet ancient history is rarely as complete as surviving records make it appear. A name missing from a royal list does not necessarily mean the person never ruled, particularly when other objects and inscriptions point to a different sequence of events. Now, researchers have brought together several such clues to argue that three rulers who were largely absent from the traditional record may have briefly occupied the Assyrian throne.The study , published in the Journal of Cuneiform Studies by Alexander Johannes Edmonds and Eckart Frahm, examines evidence from ancient tablets, inscriptions and a damaged royal statue. Their findings suggest that three previously overlooked kings may have ruled during periods of political uncertainty, potentially requiring parts of Assyria’s accepted chronology to be reconsidered.The Assyrian King List has traditionally been an important foundation for reconstructing the succession of Assyrian rulers.The problem, according to Edmonds and Frahm, is the assumption that it contains every Neo-Assyrian monarch. The researchers examined ancient evidence that does not fit comfortably into the established sequence. Rather than treating those inconsistencies simply as scribal mistakes, they considered whether they could indicate the existence of short-lived rulers who were subsequently omitted from the official record. Their study presents three separate historical scenarios involving rulers who either reigned alongside kings already known from the list or occupied gaps between them. The evidence comes from different types of surviving material, including cuneiform tablets, royal inscriptions and a damaged statue.One of the most striking cases concerns a ruler named Tiglath-pileser, who appears to have challenged his nephew, Aššur-dān III. The evidence comes in part from a clay tablet recording a royal grant issued in Tiglath-pileser's name. The tablet is dated to 762 BCE and identifies him as king of Assyria, despite the established chronology placing Aššur-dān III on the throne at that time.Edmonds and Frahm propose that this Tiglath-pileser briefly seized power around 763-762 BCE. Their reconstruction connects his rise to a period of political instability that followed a solar eclipse. He appears to have attempted to overthrow Aššur-dān III before being removed from power. His short reign could help explain why the ruler is absent from the conventional king list. The researchers argue that references to him were subsequently excluded from the official historical record, leaving only fragments of evidence behind.The second proposed king is Shalmaneser, whose existence helps explain an unusual ancient monument. A stela discovered at Tell 'Abta in Iraq had an inscription whose original royal name was later overwritten with the name of Tiglath-pileser III. For years, the alteration created a historical puzzle because the monument appeared to contain evidence that did not fit neatly into the established succession.Edmonds and Frahm argue that the mystery becomes more understandable if a previously omitted Shalmaneser is placed into the sequence. They propose that he ruled from approximately 747 to 745 BCE, immediately before Tiglath-pileser III came to power in 745 BCE. The researchers suggest that the monument's original name was deliberately replaced. This would mean the physical object itself preserves evidence of a ruler whose place in the official historical memory was later erased.The third proposed ruler, Aššur-uballiṭ, belongs to an earlier period. The researchers tentatively place his reign around 913-912 BCE, between the reigns of Tukultī-Ninurta I and Tukultī-Ninurta II. A cuneiform text provides an important clue. It describes a ceremonial vessel originally made under Tukultī-Ninurta I and later restored by Aššur-uballiṭ. Yet the established Assyrian King List contains no ruler with that name between the two Tukultī-Ninurtas.The researchers connect this evidence with a damaged royal statue discovered at the ancient city of Aššur. The statue had been decapitated, while its arms and royal insignia had also been deliberately damaged. Edmonds and Frahm argue that it may represent Aššur-uballiṭ and provide another physical trace of a ruler who was later removed from the historical record.The three cases do not simply add three names to an ancient list. They raise questions about how Assyrian political history was recorded in the first place. Edmonds and Frahm argue that the Assyrian King List may not have functioned as a completely neutral record of every ruler. Instead, they suggest it could have served as a legitimising canon of kings, with short-lived or rival rulers removed from the sequence by later authorities.All three proposed kings appear to have had extremely short reigns, with the evidence suggesting that each ruled for less than two years. Their omission could therefore have helped create a cleaner succession than the political reality actually allowed. The findings suggest that early Neo-Assyrian political history involved more rebellion, rivalry and contested succession than the traditional chronology reveals. They also demonstrate how seemingly disconnected pieces of evidence can become meaningful when examined together.Rather than completely overturning Assyrian chronology, the study challenges the assumption that the existing king list provides a complete record of the kingdom's rulers. It opens the possibility that further inconsistencies in ancient texts and monuments could reveal additional details about rulers who disappeared from the official historical memory.
Article Summary: The Assyrian King List has traditionally been an important foundation for reconstructing the succession of Assyrian rulers. The problem, according to Edmonds and Frahm, is the assumption that it contains every Neo-Assyrian monarch. The researchers examined ancient evidence that does not fit comfortably into the established sequence. Their findings suggest that three previously overlooked kings may have ruled during periods of political uncertainty.

Article Title: Scientists took 232 gravity readings across a Utah mountain and discovered 1.55 million cubic metres of ice hidden beneath loose rock, enough frozen water to fill about 600 Olympic swimming pools
Article Text:
​Timpanogos Rock Glacier ice discovery

232 gravity readings have uncovered the secret ice

How does ice get under all that rock?

The secret water reserves in a warming climate

They used Bayesian statistical modeling to generate a three-dimensional picture of the ice under the rocks. It gave an unprecedented view of the interior of Timpanogos Rock Glacier.

Why are rock glaciers important?

From a distance it looks like nothing more than a sprawling pile of rocks high in Utah’s Wasatch Range. But beneath the rubble of Mount Timpanogos is a spectacular hidden reservoir: ice enough to hold some 1.55 million cubic meters of water, which is about 600 Olympic-sized swimming pools. Now, researchers at the University of Utah have mapped this invisible ice using an unusual approach: measuring tiny variations in gravity across the rocky landscape, the university website reports. It’s the Timpanogos Rock Glacier, one of hundreds of rock glaciers in Utah. Unlike normal glaciers, which are large masses of exposed ice and snow, rock glaciers are covered by a thick mantle of loose rock. That rocky exterior is difficult to study, but below it there may be vast amounts of frozen water, the news report states. Timpanogos Rock Glacier is estimated to be around 83% ice and 17% loose rock and is particularly ice-rich. At its deepest point, the ice is buried about 150 feet beneath the surface. According to glaciologist Leif Anderson, “There’s a lot of ice hiding in Utah’s mountains.” Hikers walking over what seems to be normal rubble may be blissfully unaware that dozens of meters of ice could be underneath. Scroll down to read more about it.In fall 2024, University of Utah geologist Bronson Cvijanovich led fieldwork at the glacier to get a better sense of what was beneath the surface. The team made six trips to the site, carrying sensitive scientific equipment up a tough trail. The site is accessible from a trailhead, but it’s a five-mile hike and climb of some 3,500 feet to reach the rock glacier. The researchers used a sophisticated gravimeter to take readings at 232 locations about 25 meters apart. It measures small variations in gravitational acceleration resulting from density differences. Areas with thicker buried ice have a slightly weaker pull from gravity, because rock is much denser than ice. Scientists corrected the measurements for elevation, latitude, terrain, and gravitational effects from the Sun and Moon. They then used Bayesian statistical modeling to generate a three-dimensional picture of the ice under the rocks. It gave an unprecedented view of the interior of Timpanogos Rock Glacier.The researchers also explored yet another equally interesting question: how does a rock glacier develop ice when its surface is covered with rocks? The answer seems to be a combination of snowfall and rockfall. Rock glaciers often occur beneath steep mountain slopes and cirques where rocks frequently break loose. Large rocks falling on areas of persistent snow can bury and protect the snow from melting. This process adds ice to the rock glacier over time. Researchers found that years with heavy snowfall, cool summers and substantial rockfalls can contribute to ice accumulation. More than 70 patches of debris-covered snow still exist at Timpanogos, scientists have found.The discovery could have implications far beyond Mount Timpanogos. Utah has 836 known rock glaciers, but researchers believe there are about 50,000 rock glaciers worldwide. The authors estimate that the world's rock glaciers contain about 48 gigatons of water by using a correlation between the surface area of a rock glacier and its buried ice volume. Rock glaciers in Utah may contain about one gigaton of water, or about 815,000 acre-feet. Scientists note that not all rock glaciers are necessarily gaining ice today. Some have already lost their frozen hearts. But Timpanogos Rock Glacier seems to still be active, adding ice.Such hidden ice reserves could be especially significant to a warm, dry state like Utah. A thick layer of rock helps shield the ice below from heat and sun, potentially allowing rock glaciers to keep water around longer than exposed ice. The research also alters scientists’ view of these formations. Some rock glaciers are not just relics of ancient glacial history but are dynamic systems interacting with today's climate. So what looks from above like a normal field of rocks could be concealing a large reserve of frozen water—and new scientific tools are finally allowing scientists to see what is underneath.Images Courtesy: The University of Utah
Article Summary: Researchers at the University of Utah have mapped this invisible ice using an unusual approach: measuring tiny variations in gravity across the rocky landscape. Timpanogos Rock Glacier is estimated to be around 83% ice and 17% loose rock and is particularly ice-rich. At its deepest point, the ice is buried about 150 feet beneath the surface.

Article Title: A wooden relic that survived the sack of Jerusalem's First Temple was unearthed by archaeologists, now they are finding shocking answers
Article Text:
Image credit: Reut VilfImage source: Tel Aviv University

A preserved relic

The thick beams discovered were made of sycamore wood and as per experts, once formed part of the roof of an interior courtyardImage credit: Efrat BocherImage source: Tel Aviv University

Preserved among the ruins

In the current world, it is highly unlikely to come across intact wood that is thousands of years old and yet untouched. During an archaeological excavation in the area known as the Givati Parking Lot in the City of David, a team of researchers recently uncovered charred remains dating to the Iron Age, from the time of the destruction of Jerusalem's First Temple in 586 B.C. as per a report by AS. Alongside these fragments, researchers also found conifer wood containing numerous well-preserved growth rings.The thick beams discovered were made of sycamore wood and as per experts, once formed part of the roof of an interior courtyard. Efrat Bocher, an excavation director, said that the beams "appear to have served as the roof of an inner courtyard." "During the destruction, they collapsed onto the floor," Bocher said in a statement.They date back to roughly 2,600 years, likely the remnants of the destruction of Solomon's Temple. The discovery was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) in July. IAA officials said the wood was found "within a building that collapsed by the intense fire at the time of the First Temple's destruction."Their statement added, "What likely preserved the beams for approximately 2,600 years was plaster that melted from the building's walls, sealing the burnt wood beneath it."The big question is how they managed to survive for so long. The answer lies in the very fire that destroyed the building. When the flames consumed the structure, the timbers collapsed to the ground and were immediately covered by plaster from the walls, which the intense heat had altered. This layer of material acted as a nearly perfect protective seal, preventing the remains from disintegrating over the centuries.Researcher Johanna Regev explained that combining the analysis of these rings with modern radiocarbon testing makes it possible to determine dates with much greater precision. Until now, experts often had to work with margins of error spanning hundreds of years when dating objects this ancient. With this material, however, the time frame can be narrowed to just a decade.Solomon's Temple, also called the First Temple, was destroyed by Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 B.C., after his army captured Jerusalem following a lengthy siege. It was originally built by King Solomon in the 10th century B.C. as the permanent house for the Ark of the Covenant, according to Scripture. The destruction of Solomon's Temple ushered in the Second Temple period, the era of Judaism in which Jesus lived and practised.Experts leading the project believe that the people who returned to the city decades after the sack made a conscious decision not to clear the area, leaving the burned remains exactly where they lay. The purpose of this act may have been to keep the memory of the disaster alive, with new streets later built directly over the ashes."Preserving memory is a human need, seeking to preserve what once existed," excavation director Yiftah Shalev said in a statement. "Here we see it in its clearest form: a deliberate choice to leave ruins in place as a testament to the destruction and build the new layer over them."This historic discovery also coincides on the calendar with the traditional dates commemorating the fall of the ancient city at the hands of the Babylonians. The event is still remembered in the region each year through Tisha B’Av, which involves various days of mourning and fasting.In a statement, Bocher called the discovery "deeply moving." It "makes you feel that you are witnessing the very moment of destruction, the moment when it all happened," she said.Jerusalem, known as the Eternal City, is the setting of countless notable archaeological discoveries per year. Last year, archaeologists in Jerusalem uncovered the longest and best-preserved section of the city's Hasmonean-era wall. And earlier this year, excavators uncovered a "mysterious and impressive" ancient tunnel near Jerusalem's biblical-era Kingdom of Judah.
Article Summary: Archaeologists in Jerusalem have found charred remains dating back to the Iron Age. The remains were found in the Givati Parking Lot in the City of David. They date back to roughly 2,600 years, likely the remnants of the destruction of Solomon's Temple in 586 B.C.

Article Title: Hindu priest arrested in Canada for sexually assaulting woman under guise of healing

Rajendranauth Doodnauth MARAJ,/Image: Durham Regional Police

A US-based Hindu priest has been arrested in Oshawa, Canada, for sexually assaulting a woman under the guise of a religious healing ceremony.Police said the victim and her family had hired the priest, identified as Rajendranauth Doodnauth Maraj, 50, to travel from the US to perform a Hindu religious ceremony. Maraj is from Richmond Hill, New York.According to Durham Regional Police, Maraj told the woman that she was possessed by evil spirits and convinced her that she needed a specific ceremony to be healed. Maraj was later taken into custody .He has been charged with one count of sexual assault and was held for a bail hearing.

Article Title: US college student shot dead by police after knocking on wrong house amid burglary call
Article Text:
22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania. (AP Photo)

A 22-year-old college student was shot and killed by police in Pennsylvania after he mistakenly went to the wrong house and was waiting for his friends to pick him up, his father said.Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in, CNN reported citing Montgomery County district attorney’s office. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead.Pysher’s father, Glen Pysher, said his son had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.According to what his son’s friends told him, Pysher took a wrong turn through the woods and mistakenly went to a house he believed belonged to a friend.Pysher was carrying only his phone and a backpack with clothes and a few beers, his father said. He allegedly tried to open the door and called out, “Hey! Open the door!” believing he was at his friend’s home.After realising the mistake, Pysher sat on the back porch and contacted his friends.They then started heading to the house to pick him up.His friends later saw police and emergency vehicles at the location and initially believed Pysher would be arrested for public drunkenness. Instead, he had been shot.Pysher’s father said his son was on a FaceTime call with his friends at 12:32 am, while police were dispatched at 12:30 am and arrived at 12:34 am, according to a Montgomery County Department of Public Safety dispatch record.The father questioned what happened during the brief interval before his son was shot.Upper Pottsgrove Township Police Chief Al Werner has declined to release details, including the names of the officers involved, pending the investigation.The Montgomery County Detective Bureau is investigating the shooting, the district attorney’s office said.Pysher was due to begin his senior year at Saint Elizabeth University in New Jersey, where he planned to play baseball. He hoped to become a high school history teacher and coach after graduating.His father described him as kind-hearted and loving, saying former teammates, coaches and others had reached out with memories of him since his death.The family has also said it has received little information from police.Pysher’s father said he was recently told he could collect his son’s favourite black shoes so they could be used for his burial, but was later told officials needed to consider whether they could release them.
Article Summary: Police in Upper Pottsgrove Township, northwest of Philadelphia, responded around 12:30 am Sunday to a 911 call reporting a possible break-in. Officers found Glenwood Pysher IV at the rear of the house and later shot him dead. He had been out with friends at several bars before they split up to spend the night at two different homes.
