Article Title: 'It's your sense of entitlement': US officials slam Indian-origin entrepreneur Ankit Gupta over H-1B comments
Article Text:
Indian-origin serial entrepreneur Ankit Gupta, general partner of YC, is at the center of a major social media storm over his comments on H-1B which he deleted later.

Who is Ankit Gupta ? What is the latest H-1B controversy?

Ankit Gupta was accused of deriding Americans as he was defending the H-1B immigrant culture.

White House official reacts, YC CEO issues statement

Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest, following which Gupta made his X account private. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement". Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.Gupta, a distinguished computer scientist from Harvard, is a serial entrepreneur and currently a partner of Y Combinator. Before joining YC, he was the co-founder and CTO of Reveries Labs. The controversy that he landed in stemmed from his comment on JD Vance's post."If an American corporation needs workers, it should hire and train Americans," Vice President JD Vance wrote on X, reacting to the Donald Trump administration's new H-1B visa fee. "in a win for the woke left DEI is back," Ankit Gupta commented, suggesting that if Americans have to be hired because they are Americans and not because of their skill, then it is DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inlcusion) only.The now-deleted post and the sarcasm did not go down well with America First commentators, and then it came to the notice of the DOL's Inspector General."Ankit Gupta thinks hiring Americans first—in America—is “DEI.” No, Ankit. It’s called putting your own citizens first. American companies. American jobs. American workers first. If that offends you, the problem isn’t America. It’s your sense of entitlement," D'Esposito said.As Gupta defended the H-1B hiring by Silicon Valley, he asked one commentator: 'what elements of H-1B immigrant culture do you not like? is it the willingness to work long hours? Or perhaps the education focus of their children?""Leaving trash everywhere, scamming people, endemic pathological dishonesty, atrocious aesthetic taste, need I go on," the commentator replied. "It's giving flyover country," Gupta wrote. Social media users started flagging this comment as a racist attack aimed at rural white Americans and asked YC to take action against Gupta."Hey @ycombinator this is a racist attack aimed at rural White Americans. Your policies mention that you do not tolerate any racism. It states that racial discrimination is a fireable offense. When can we expect you to fire Ankit Gupta?" one wrote.Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson, responded to the controversy and called YCombinator "a front for the far left"."Y Combinator is a supposed champion of “Little Tech” but perhaps they’re nothing more than a front for the far left. I’m deeply uncomfortable with wealthy investors attacking American workers like this. I’m afraid it’s increasingly obvious to many people that individuals such as this guy do not have the best interests of America and her citizens in mind," Ferguson wrote, referring to Gupta."The purpose of the American economy is to promote the general welfare of American workers, not provide jobs for the rest of the world," he said.Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan issued a statement saying that YC supports hiring and funding Americans.
Article Summary: Indian-American entrepreneur Ankit Gupta landed in a soup after his H-1B comments on social media that stirred the hornet's nest. Inspector General of the US Department of Labor took note of Gupta's comment and slammed him publicly, calling out what he termed as his "sense of entitlement" Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission of the United States Andrew Ferguson said individuals like Gupta do not have the best interests of Americans in their minds.

Article Title: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's US event organiser AHEAD’s X account restored after brief suspension
Article Text:
The X account of RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s US event organiser, which was suspended, has now been restored.

The X (formerly Twitter) account of American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD), which is organising Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat ’s event at New York’s Madison Square Garden, has been restored after a brief suspension. AHEAD said it believes opponents used automated activity to get the account blocked and thanked X for restoring it.“We are back up! We got ‘botted’ by misguided opponents who tried to game the X algorithm and get our handle blocked. A big thank you to @X @Support for the prompt response, restoring our account and clearing out the bots. Now, back to what really matters: celebrating Universal Harmony and Universal Oneness @Uni1ness,” AHEAD said in a post on X.The account, operating under the handle @AheadForum1, had earlier become unavailable to users on Thursday. AHEAD had initially said it believed the suspension may have occurred in error.Bhagwat is scheduled to address the “Universal Oneness Celebration” at the Infosys Theatre at Madison Square Garden on August 29. The programme is expected to draw around 5,000 Indian Americans as part of the RSS's global outreach during its centenary yearEarlier this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he did not support the planned event, while acknowledging that his office may not have the authority to cancel a private gathering.“I don’t support the rally, but I don’t know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,” Mamdani told reporters on Tuesday.Mamdani's comments have triggered criticism among sections of the Indian-American diaspora and have also drawn opposing reactions from Indian political parties. His remarks came as left-liberal groups criticised the event and called for its cancellation.The controversy has also prompted a security advisory from the Hindu American Foundation (HAF), a US-based non-profit organisation. HAF urged people attending the event to remain vigilant, stay aware of their surroundings and keep interactions civil.HAF said the advisory followed attempts by activists targeting Hindu Americans to disrupt and cancel the celebration.It also called on Mamdani to ensure the safety of people attending the event.The event has also drawn scrutiny from the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), which has urged the US government to consider sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials it alleges are involved in religious freedom violations in India.“We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat and making him ineligible for future entry into the United States,” the body said.The commission is chaired by Pakistani-American Asif Mahmood.India's Ministry of External Affairs has previously rejected USCIRF's assessments, accusing the body of bias and questioning its credibility. During an August 21 press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the commission had made what he described as “incorrect and provocative statements about India” for years.“We all know this is a biased institution. For years, it has made incorrect and provocative statements about India. We should ignore such institutions, as they have their own agendas and lack credibility,” Jaiswal said.
Article Summary: The X (formerly Twitter) account of American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) has been restored after a brief suspension. AHEAD is organising Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat ’s event at New York’s Madison Square Garden. The account, operating under the handle @AheadForum1, had earlier become unavailable to users.

Article Title: Trump admin seeks US Supreme Court nod for policy banning transgender from military service
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump.

The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in a legal battle over its policy banning transgender people from serving in the military, seeking to clear the way for the discharge of about two dozen service members.According to The Washington Post, the administration has filed an emergency request seeking to lift a lower-court injunction that has allowed 28 transgender service members to remain in the military while their lawsuit challenging the policy proceeds.The case stems from an executive order signed by President Donald Trump shortly after he returned to office, directing the Pentagon to remove transgender service members. The Defence Department formally implemented the policy in February 2025.The administration argued that the executive branch has broad authority to determine military eligibility and that courts should defer to the Defence Department on questions of military readiness and effectiveness. Solicitor General D John Sauer urged the Supreme Court to intervene before the case reaches a full trial.The transgender service members, led by Army Reserve Second Lieutenant Nicolas Talbott, have argued that removing them before a final ruling would cause irreparable harm.In June, a divided three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld protections for the 28 service members, finding that the policy appeared to be driven by prejudice rather than military necessity.The administration's latest request marks a fresh escalation in the legal fight. The Supreme Court's conservative majority had previously allowed the administration to temporarily enforce the transgender military ban in an emergency ruling in May 2025.The Supreme Court is expected to decide this fall whether to take up the case for full review. If it agrees, a ruling could come during the court's upcoming term and potentially determine the constitutionality of Trump's transgender military policy.
Article Summary: The administration has filed an emergency request seeking to lift a lower-court injunction that has allowed 28 transgender service members to remain in the military. The Supreme Court is expected to decide this fall whether to take up the case for full review. If it agrees, a ruling could come during the court's upcoming term and potentially determine the constitutionality of the policy.

Article Title: In 1974, a biologist moved to a Washington island because one marsh supported 80 bird species; he devoted the rest of his life to it, and neighbours later created a wildlife preserve
Article Text:
An aerial view of Orcas Island, one of the islands that make up the San Juan Islands in northern Puget Sound. Its coastline is a mix of sandy and rocky beaches and shallow and deep harbours, which provide habitats for a wide variety of plants and animals. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

An unusually busy patch of wetland

Orcas Island beach. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A preserve built after his death

When Dr. Frank Richardson retired from the University of Washington in 1972, he did not slow down. He shifted his fieldwork from museum collections to a wetland near his home, trading decades of specimen cataloguing for hours spent watching live birds in the marsh. Two years later, he made the shift permanent, settling on Orcas Island in the San Juan Islands and turning that single wetland into the last great subject of his working life. The marsh he studied now bears his name as a protected wildlife preserve, a legacy his neighbours created after his death.Richardson spent his career as a professor of zoology at the University of Washington and headed the ornithology division at the Burke Museum, which held one of the country's largest bird specimen collections. After stepping down from that post in 1972, he did not retire from birdwatching itself, spending time studying bird life on Cypress Island before settling permanently on Orcas Island in 1974 with his wife, Dorothy, the San Juan Preservation Trust , which now manages the reserve built around his work.Richardson's academic training left him with a habit of counting and cataloguing what he saw rather than simply observing it. Near Deer Harbour, he soon began studying a modest wetland close to his new home.Richardson found that the marsh supported an unusually high number of bird species. Despite covering only a small stretch of land near Channel Road, the site supported roughly 80 different species of birds moving through or nesting there across the seasons, an unusually high count for a wetland of its size.The marsh sat along the Pacific Flyway, the migratory corridor that carries waterfowl and shorebirds up and down the West Coast each year. That helped explain why so many species stopped there.Richardson came to believe that counting birds alone was not enough. He had watched habitats disappear across the region during his academic career, and he concluded that the long-term survival of many species depended on protecting the specific pieces of ground they relied on, not just studying them from a distance. That conviction led him to land conservation work in the San Juan Islands during his final years, applying decades of ornithological training to protect a single marsh.Richardson died in 1985, but his work to protect the marsh continued after his death. The following year, neighbours Bob and Meg Connor donated a seven-acre conservation easement covering the eastern portion of the wetland, a gift that initiated the effort to establish the Frank Richardson Wildfowl Preserve. A memorial plaque to Richardson now sits on a boulder along Channel Road at the edge of the marsh, marking the spot for visitors who stop to look out over the water.Richardson's influence on Orcas Island extended beyond the marsh itself. Colleagues remembered him as a generous mentor, including wildlife artist Tony Angell, who said a chance friendship with Richardson at the Burke Museum shaped his career studying and illustrating Northwest birds, as documented by HistoryLink , the Washington State history resource. Angell later credited those early outings with Richardson, searching for carving stone along the Upper Skagit and examining study skins at the museum, as the spark that led him to a lifetime of wildlife art.That same generosity was reflected in how Richardson was remembered professionally after he died in 1985. An obituary published the following year in The Auk , the journal of the American Ornithologists' Union, noted the breadth of Richardson's contributions to Pacific Northwest ornithology over a career that ultimately outlasted his formal retirement by well over a decade.Today the preserve remains a working wetland rather than a museum piece, still hosting the same seasonal traffic of migrating wildfowl that first caught Richardson's attention half a century ago. Part of its acreage lies in upland forest across the road from the marsh itself, and a short pedestrian path leads visitors up to a screened viewpoint overlooking the water. It is a small piece of ground by conservation standards, but it stands as the direct result of one retired professor's decision to keep doing fieldwork long after his job ended and of neighbours who chose to protect that work after he was gone.
Article Summary: Dr Frank Richardson spent his career as a zoology professor at the University of Washington. When he retired in 1972, he moved to Orcas Island in the San Juan Islands. He began studying a small wetland near Deer Harbour, which supported an unusually high number of bird species. The marsh now bears his name as a protected wildlife preserve, a legacy his neighbours created after his death.

Article Title: In 1946, Eisenhower’s brothers gave their Abilene family home to a foundation; it opened to visitors the next year
Article Text:
Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later became the 34th president of the United States, lived in the house until he left for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1911 | Wikimedia Commons

Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later became the 34th president of the United States, lived in the house until he left for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1911 | Wikimedia Commons

The house where six Eisenhower boys grew up

The brothers decided to preserve the family home

Visitors arrived within months

The Eisenhower family home, Abilene, Kansas | Wikimedia Commons

The home survived a major flood

Ida Eisenhower died in 1946, when her six sons gave the family home in Abilene, Kansas, to the Eisenhower Foundation. The house opened to the public in June 1947 and was preserved with the furniture and household details that remained after their mother’s death. The house had been the Eisenhower family home since 1898. David and Ida Eisenhower bought the six-room property on Southeast Fourth Street from David’s brother, Abraham Lincoln Eisenhower, and raised their six sons there. Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later became the 34th president of the United States, lived in the house until he left for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1911. According to the Eisenhower Presidential Library , the family remained in the house until Ida died in 1946.The property covered about 2.5 to 3 acres and included a barn, chicken house, smokehouse, outhouse, orchard, strawberry patch and kitchen garden. In 1900, Ida's father-in-law, Jacob Eisenhower, moved in with the family. Two bedrooms and a walk-through closet were added to the east side of the house, and an indoor bathroom was added around 1908, followed by a small kitchen, pantry and enclosed back porch in 1915.TheEisenhower Presidential Library records those changes in its history of the property.Dwight was one of the six brothers raised in the house. He left Abilene for West Point in 1911, but the rest of the family continued living there for decades. His father, David, died in 1942, and Ida remained in the house until her death four years later.After Ida's death, the house could have become another privately held family property; instead, the Eisenhower brothers agreed to give it to the Eisenhower Foundation, which had been established in 1945 to create a memorial to General Eisenhower and honor World War II veterans. The foundation's early records provide a more detailed account of the transfer. In its 1947 annual meeting report, the Kansas Historical Society recorded that Milton Eisenhower acted for the surviving brothers when the property was deeded to the foundation in June 1946. One of the six brothers, Arthur, had died in 1942.A new roof and paint were among the early repairs, and the primary intention was to preserve the rooms and possessions as they had been during Ida Eisenhower's lifetime. The decision meant visitors could see more than an old house associated with a future president. The furnishings, books, piano, kitchen equipment and bedroom furniture remained in place. The 1947 Kansas Historical Society account described the rooms as they had been left by Ida.The Eisenhower Foundation opened the house to the public on June 22, 1947. More than 500 people visited on the opening day, according to the Eisenhower Foundation , and the event was broadcast by seven radio stations. A Kansas Historical Society account published in 1947 said more than 12,000 people had toured the house during its first 120 days, with visitors arriving from every U.S. state and 11 foreign countries. The foundation hired guides to take visitors through the rooms.At that point, Eisenhower was still a military figure rather than a former president, and his presidency eventually began in January 1953, after he won the 1952 election. The house continued to be associated with him as his public career developed. It was eventually incorporated into the larger presidential library and museum complex in Abilene.In July 1951, flooding damaged the basement and ruined part of its rock foundation. The first floor managed to escape the flood damage, but the structure needed substantial work. Repairs were completed several years later, and the home was rededicated in November 1956. The White House Historical Association notes that later maintenance, including work on climate and security systems, exterior painting and reroofing, has helped retain its appearance.The property was eventually transferred from the Eisenhower Foundation to the federal government in 1966 and became part of the presidential library system. The Texas Historical Commission also records that the foundation operated the house until the transfer. The Eisenhower Presidential Library says the house is furnished as it was when Ida died in 1946. Many of the furnishings are original, while some have been moved to accommodate visitors.A preservation project completed in 2022 included exterior lead-paint abatement and maintenance work. The home now provides scheduled tours from Tuesday through Sunday, with tours limited to 10 people at a time. The house at Southeast Fourth Street remains part of the Eisenhower Presidential Library, Museum and Boyhood Home in Abilene. The building where the Eisenhower family lived from 1898 until Ida's death in 1946 has been receiving visitors since 1947.
Article Summary: Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later became the 34th president of the United States, lived in the house until he left for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1911. David and Ida Eisenhower bought the six-room property on Southeast Fourth Street from David’s brother, Abraham Lincoln Eisenhower, and raised their six sons there. The house opened to the public in June 1947.

Article Title: In 1832, a New York merchant built a house with a hidden 2-foot-wide passage; researchers now link it to the Underground Railroad
Article Text:
Representative Image of a hidden passage concealed behind furniture in a 19th-century house linked to Underground Railroad history (AI-generated image)

Why historians believe the passage was connected to the Underground Railroad

Why the discovery adds another chapter to New York's abolitionist history

How the hidden passage survived inside the Merchant's House

What the discovery means for Manhattan

For decades, visitors to Manhattan's Merchant's House Museum walked past a built-in chest of drawers without knowing the full significance of the narrow passage concealed behind it. After two years of research, historians concluded that the passage was likely used as a hiding place for people escaping slavery. The passage is roughly 2 feet square and descends about 15 feet from the second floor toward the ground floor. The museum announced the finding in February 2026, describing the 1832 Merchant's House as the earliest known site of Underground Railroad activity in New York City. The house was built by Joseph Brewster, a wealthy merchant and abolitionist, and the museum says the passage appears to have been incorporated into the building when it was constructed. Its physical existence was known before the recent research; what changed was the understanding of what the unusual space may have been used for.According to the Merchant's House Museum, the passage is an unusual feature of the 1832 building and has no obvious domestic purpose. Its entrance is concealed beneath a built-in chest of drawers on the second floor, while the narrow shaft extends downward through the house.Researchers examined the architecture alongside historical evidence about Brewster and New York's abolitionist movement. Patrick Ciccone, an architectural historian involved in the research, emphasised that Brewster's background was significant because wealthy white New Yorkers who openly opposed slavery were unusual at the time. He described Brewster as the builder of the house, meaning he was in a position to make deliberate choices about its construction. The museum has therefore interpreted the passage as a space intended to conceal freedom-seekers, while continuing to distinguish that conclusion from a surviving document that explicitly states who used the passage or exactly how often it was used.The passage was constructed during a complicated period in New York. Although New York State had abolished slavery in 1827, the city's economy remained closely connected to the slaveholding South. At the same time, New York had an active abolitionist movement led in large part by free Black residents, alongside white abolitionists who worked within the movement. People involved in helping those escaping slavery often had to operate discreetly. The Underground Railroad was not a literal railroad but a loose network of people, homes and other locations that helped freedom-seekers travel toward places where they could live outside the institution of slavery. The Merchant's House passage provides a rare physical reminder of that history. Much of what is known about the Underground Railroad comes from documentary accounts, oral histories and later historical research. Intact spaces that may have been used for concealment are considerably rarer.The Merchant's House was constructed in 1832 and later became the home of the Tredwell family, who occupied the property for almost a century. The building eventually became a museum in 1936 and is now one of New York City's best-preserved examples of a 19th-century merchant family's home. The concealed passage survived largely intact within the building. Its entrance is hidden beneath a chest of drawers, making it difficult to notice as part of the house's ordinary interior. The recent research brought together the physical evidence inside the building with historical information about Brewster and the abolitionist networks operating in New York during the period. The museum subsequently presented the passage as evidence of the house's connection to the Underground Railroad.The Merchant's House Museum now identifies the property as the earliest known Underground Railroad site in New York City. That distinction is significant because Manhattan played an important role in the abolitionist movement, yet comparatively few physical spaces associated with the city's Underground Railroad history have survived in an intact form. The discovery also broadens the story told by the museum itself. For decades, the Merchant's House was primarily understood through the domestic history of the Tredwell family and their household. The hidden passage adds another layer to that history, connecting the building to the wider struggle over slavery and freedom in 19th-century New York. For historians, the most important question may now be what else can be established about the passage. The architecture suggests a deliberate attempt at concealment, while Brewster's abolitionist views provide historical context. But identifying the specific people who may have sheltered there and documenting how the space was actually used will require further research.
Article Summary: The passage is hidden behind a chest of drawers on the second floor of the Merchant's House Museum in New York City. The house was built by Joseph Brewster, a wealthy merchant and abolitionist, and the passage appears to have been incorporated into the building when it was constructed. Researchers examined the architecture alongside historical evidence about Brewster and New York's abolitionist movement.

Article Title: In 2002, Alabama architecture students stacked 72,000 worn carpet tiles into the walls of a family home; Rural Studio has now built more than 200 projects
Article Text: A house in Alabama contains walls adorned with 72,000 individual stacked tiles held in compression by a heavy wooden-ring beam. Belonging to the Harris family, the abode contains a bedroom above and a tornado shelter below. The minds behind the idea trace back to Rural Studio, an off-campus design-build program, rooted in Hale County and part of the School of Architecture, Planning and Landscape Architecture of Auburn University, according to the studio's website.Known as the Lucy Carpet House, it was constructed in 2002 by a team of six students developing a concept assigned by the studio co-founder Sambo Mockbee. The project was a charity house for Lucy and Anderson Harris and their children. It was funded by Interface Carpet. The company donated $30,000, as well as 72,000 pounds of post-consumer carpet tiles. The tiles were held in storage for 7 years to ensure they no longer off-gassed.By creating a system of stacked carpet tiles to make the walls of the house, they were able to conserve enough of the budget to build Lucy the only thing she asked for: a place to pray. For this, Lucy’s bedroom is a sculptural tower, open only to the sky.As she lies in her bed, Lucy can look up at the sky and enjoy the play of light and shadow on the faceted surfaces of her prayer tower.In 1993 two Auburn professors came to this corner of the state, called Hale County, when Newbern was little more than a few dusty streets and churches, and many people were living in precarious old houses. The architects’ proposition was simple: let our students live here and learn by doing, and we will help to build your civic infrastructure. To date, the studio has built more than 200 projects and educated more than 1,200 students in the Black Belt.Around four dozen students are invited to attend each year to participate in this context-based service-learning curriculum, where students live and work alongside our neighbours, finding solutions together. The design-build program challenges students to consider not what can be built but rather what should be built. Their final projects are assessed on whether their structures can stand the test of time, surviving the notorious tornadoes of “Dixie Alley” and the extremes of summer and winter here.“We encourage aspiring young architects to address the ethical responsibility for the social, political, and environmental consequences of what they design and build,” said Andrew Freear, Rural Studio Director.In 2004, Rural Studio began the 20K Initiative to focus students’ efforts on creating single-family detached housing that keeps material and labour costs to an affordable minimum. That program and other research projects have yielded a body of knowledge that illuminates a scalable solution to the problem of housing affordability. The studio’s latest effort, the Front Porch Initiative, is working toward that goal with the help of several partners. Through housing designs refined from the 20K Initiative as well as novel financing mechanisms being developed with partners, Rural Studio aims to fundamentally shift models and practices for affordable housing.It might sound idyllic but Newbern is also at the sharp end of rural life. As in many small, isolated communities in the American South, as well as Italy, Spain and elsewhere, old families are dying out or departing for cities in search of work and opportunity. For generations, there was little civic infrastructure to keep people rooted and local leaders now seek out the services of Rural Studio to arrest their town’s decline.Over a period of 30 years, waves of students have created the vast Lions Park in nearby Greensboro, turned a defunct bank building into Newbern Library, which became the first place in town where high-speed internet was available to the public, and built Newbern’s town hall out of cypress logs.Today, the program runs the Front Porch Initiative, working with housing providers and organisations nationwide to scale their high-performance, affordable rural housing designs into commercial reality.
Article Summary: The Lucy Carpet House was constructed in 2002 by a team of six students developing a concept assigned by the studio co-founder Sambo Mockbee. The project was a charity house for Lucy and Anderson Harris and their children. It was funded by Interface Carpet. The tiles were held in storage for 7 years to ensure they no longer off-gassed.

Article Title: A New Orleans couple found a 2,000-year-old Roman tombstone in their backyard; the FBI traced it to Italy and returned it 80 years later
Article Text:
A long-lost ancient Roman artifact reappears in a New Orleans backyard, PC: D. Ryan Gray/Preservation Resource Center of New Orleans

Asclepius

How researchers identified the missing Roman tombstone

How a family connection revealed how the Roman stone reached New Orleans

What Sextus Congenius Verus's gravestone tells us about Roman life

Asclepius

How the Roman tombstone is being returned to Italy

Where Sextus Congenius Verus's gravestone belongs

In early 2025, Daniella Santoro, an anthropologist at Tulane University, and her partner, Aaron Lorenz, were clearing weeds behind their home in New Orleans' historic Carrollton neighbourhood when they uncovered a marble slab covered in Latin writing. Santoro contacted D. Ryan Gray, an archaeologist at the University of New Orleans, who shared photographs of the stone with Harald Stadler, an archaeologist at the University of Innsbruck, and Susann Lusnia, a classical archaeologist at Tulane. Lusnia recognised the inscription as an ancient Roman funerary monument. The stone commemorated Sextus Congenius Verus, a 42-year-old sailor who had served for 22 years aboard a ship called the. Further research established that the marble monument had once belonged to the collection of the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia, Italy, where it had eventually been recorded as missing. Its discovery transformed an unremarkable garden stone into a nearly 2,000-year-old artefact with a traceable history.According to the FBI's New Orleans field office, the inscription and physical characteristics of the marble allowed researchers to connect the New Orleans discovery with a funerary monument missing from the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia. The museum is located in the Italian coastal city of Civitavecchia, northwest of Rome.Once the identification was established, Santoro and the researchers worked with authorities to return the artefact to Italy. The FBI's Art Crime Team became involved in the repatriation process. Researchers initially considered whether the monument might have disappeared during the upheaval surrounding World War II. Civitavecchia was heavily damaged by Allied bombing during the war, creating the possibility that objects from the museum's collection could have been displaced during the destruction. The circumstances of the stone's disappearance, however, remained uncertain, and the eventual discovery in Louisiana provided a much clearer trail than researchers had previously had.The breakthrough came after news of the discovery became public. Erin Scott O'Brien, who had previously lived at the New Orleans property, learned about the Roman monument and immediately recognised the stone from her family's history. The artefact had belonged to her grandparents. Her grandfather, Charles Paddock, had served in Italy during World War II, and the stone eventually made its way into the family's possession. O'Brien did not know that it was an ancient Roman funerary monument. In 2004, she placed the stone in the garden of the New Orleans property. She later explained that the family had planted a tree and decided to put the unusual stone outside in the garden as part of the new home's landscaping. For years, the monument remained there without anyone realising what it was. It was only after Santoro and Lorenz uncovered it beneath the vegetation and archaeologists examined the inscription that its true age and history came to light. The family has not established exactly how Paddock acquired the monument in Italy. It remains possible that he purchased it, obtained it through another transaction or brought it home as a wartime souvenir, but there is no definitive family record explaining how it left Italy.The inscription provides a remarkably specific glimpse into the life of the man it commemorates. Sextus Congenius Verus was 42 when he died and had spent 22 years serving aboard the. Rather than commemorating a famous emperor or military commander, the monument belonged to an individual whose name and occupation might otherwise have disappeared from the historical record. The inscription preserves details about his age and long career at sea, offering researchers a small but tangible window into the lives of ordinary people within the Roman world. The marble also demonstrates why inscriptions can be so valuable to archaeologists. Even when an artefact becomes separated from its original archaeological context, the information carved into its surface can provide enough evidence to identify both the person it commemorates and the institution that once held it. In this case, those words survived nearly 2,000 years and ultimately helped turn an anonymous garden stone into an identifiable Roman monument.After researchers established the stone's connection to the Italian museum, the artefact entered the process of repatriation through cooperation between American and Italian authorities. The FBI's Art Crime Team assisted with the return, with the monument ultimately intended to go back to the institution from which it had disappeared. The return is part of a broader effort by the United States and Italy to recover archaeological and cultural objects that have been removed from their countries of origin. For the Roman funerary monument, however, the journey is unusually personal. The stone travelled from the ancient Roman world to an Italian museum, disappeared from the collection and eventually crossed the Atlantic before spending years in an ordinary New Orleans garden.The monument is expected to return to the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia, where it can once again be preserved and studied in the country from which it disappeared. For the researchers who identified it, the discovery demonstrates how easily an ancient artefact can become detached from its history. The stone spent years looking like an ordinary piece of marble in a New Orleans garden, while the inscription beneath the surface carried the name of a Roman sailor who lived almost 2,000 years ago. What began with a couple clearing vegetation behind their home ultimately connected archaeologists in Louisiana, Austria and Italy, a missing museum artefact, and a World War II family story. The stone's journey from ancient Rome to Louisiana and, eventually, back toward Italy is now part of the history preserved alongside the monument itself.
Article Summary: The stone commemorated Sextus Congenius Verus, a 42-year-old sailor who had served for 22 years aboard a ship called the. The marble monument had once belonged to the collection of the National Archaeological Museum in Civitavecchia, Italy. Researchers initially considered whether the monument might have disappeared during the upheaval surrounding World War II.

Article Title: A former Illinois elementary school closed in 2014; its site has now become a $1.35 million fully accessible park with an inclusive playground, walking paths and a new splash pad
Article Text:
A former school

A new playground

Poll Vote & Share your view What feature of the new Cooke Park are you most excited about? Inclusive playground Splash pad Picnic shelter Walking paths 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

On August 26 at 11:30, roughly 75 people gathered at Cooke Park for the official ribbon-cutting, capping a years-long transformation of the former Cooke Elementary School property into a fully accessible neighbourhood park. The ceremony, conducted by the Galesburg Area Chamber of Commerce, took place with the new splash pad running behind the crowd, water spraying and a light mist drifting over the gathering. The $1.352 million project includes an inclusive playground, a picnic shelter, restrooms, a bicycle repair station, walking paths and a parking area, along with the splash pad that was completed this month, according to WGIL.com.In attendance were state legislators, Mayor Peter Schwartzman, four City Council members, city officials and members of the public. Among those giving remarks were Mayor Schwartzman, Ward 4 Alderman Dwight White, whose ward includes the park, State Senator Mike Halpin, State Representative Dan Swanson, and Director of Parks and Recreation Don Miles. Several people who helped lead the push for the park also spoke, including Gayla Pacheco, Karen Ford-Kelley and Stephanie Jackson Grimes.Schwartzman, who has served as mayor for a little over five years, called the ceremony one of the proudest moments of his time in office.“This is a testament to good government, when all different levels of government, from state to local, and then the local community, work together and partner on a project that will have meaning not only immediately, but in the distant future,” Schwartzman said. "There are hundreds of people who played a role in making this happen. I thank you all, and may this park last another hundred years," he added.For several people at Wednesday's ceremony, the site carried much more significance and history. Cooke Elementary School operated on the property for decades before closing in 2014, and a handful of attendees who grew up nearby shared memories from their own school days there.White attended Cooke School from second through sixth grade. He said he still carries a scar from his time on the playground. “I scarred my leg over here chasing a boy ’cause I liked the girl,” White said. “It’s just so many great memories. Baseball out here, I tried out for Little League over here. It was just a place for the community.”White said he hopes the new park will do for the whole city what the old school grounds once did for his neighbourhood. “There’ll be some people over here that came from the north side of town, and they’re gonna meet some kid from the south side of town, and they don’t know where they’re from, and they’re gonna become friends,” White said. “That’s what this is gonna do, I hope.”Margaret Gimenez, who attended Cooke School in the 1940s, said she and a friend, Darlene Howard, were the first girls to serve as patrol guards at the school after she asked the principal why only boys held the role. “I said, ‘How come you don’t have girl patrol boys?'” Gimenez said. “She says, ‘You want to be one?’ I said, ‘Yeah.'”Gimenez said the school grounds had none of the equipment found at the new park. “We didn’t have swings or nothing. We had a monkey bar,” Gimenez said. “I’m so happy that (Pacheco) took the initiative to do this, and I know it was hard work. I’m proud of her.”The city purchased the former school property in December 2022 to create a neighbourhood park that is accessible, inclusive and welcoming to all residents. The site was chosen after strong public support for more recreational amenities on Galesburg’s southwest side.Pacheco, a Galesburg native who grew up near the school, is widely credited with spearheading the push to build the park. She said the idea grew out of conversations during the Heart & Soul community planning process around 2021 and 2022.“The thing that people were asking for was free things to do,” Pacheco said. She began working with the city around 2022 to explore turning the vacant site into a park, using a $500,000 Open Space Land Acquisition and Development grant, administered by the Illinois Department of Natural Resources (IDNR), matched by the City of Galesburg. The addition of the splash pad was made possible through a $250,000 Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity (DCEO) grant secured with support from State Senator Mike Halpin and private donations raised by the citizen-led Cooke Park Project group.Pacheco said her favourite feature is the new splash pad. “I really love those butterflies,” she said. “It reminds me of art.” Reflecting on the years of work behind the project, Pacheco credited the people around her. “It takes a village,” Pacheco said. “If you have really good family and friends, I think you can get anything done.”“We are extremely grateful to the State of Illinois, IDNR, Senator Halpin and the dedicated members of the Cooke Park project group whose advocacy and fundraising brought this project to life,” said Eric Hanson, City Manager. “Seeing children and families already enjoying the playground—and now the new splash pad—is a testament to what our community can achieve together.”
Article Summary: The $1.352 million project includes an inclusive playground, a picnic shelter, restrooms, a bicycle repair station, walking paths and a parking area. Cooke Elementary School operated on the property for decades before closing in 2014. The city purchased the former school property in December 2022 to create a neighbourhood park that is accessible and welcoming to all residents.

Article Title: Rakshabandhan in NYC: Zohran Mamdani celebrates with South Asian seniors
Article Text:
Mamdani linked the spirit of Raksha Bandhan to his broader vision for New York City, calling on residents to extend the values of care and solidarity beyond the festival.
